title: Does he deserve it?
topic: Equality and fair treatment of patients
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in cardiology. Mr Dale, 61, has angina and has been referred for coronary angiography and possible stenting. He still smokes 20 cigarettes a day.

In the team meeting, your consultant says, "Why should he get a stent if he won't stop smoking? He doesn't deserve it."
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Ask whether smoking changes the benefit of the procedure.
options.brief: Refocuses the decision on clinical grounds.
options.detailed: Smoking can affect the risks and benefits of treatment, which is a legitimate clinical consideration. Asking this respectfully moves the discussion from deserving to clinical judgement.

options.text: Offer Mr Dale support to stop smoking.
options.brief: Helps his health whatever is decided.
options.detailed: Stopping smoking is one of the most effective things he can do for his heart. Offering support, without making it a condition, helps him.

options.text: Agree with the consultant, as smoking caused his disease.
options.brief: Judging patients by lifestyle isn't fair.
options.detailed: Smoking contributed, but many conditions are linked to lifestyle. Withholding care on this basis would be discriminatory.

options.text: Say respectfully that care shouldn't depend on 'deserving' it.
options.detailed: Treatment decisions should be based on clinical need and benefit, not judgements about lifestyle. Saying so politely is part of professional practice.

options.text: Tell Mr Dale that the consultant doesn't think he deserves a stent.
options.brief: Undermines the team and distresses him.
options.detailed: This would cause him distress and damage his trust, before any decision has been made.

options.text: Report the consultant to the GMC.
options.brief: Disproportionate for a comment in a meeting.
options.detailed: The comment was inappropriate, but it should be addressed in discussion first.

options.text: Tell Mr Dale he must stop smoking before he can have the procedure.
options.brief: Imposes a condition that hasn't been agreed.
options.detailed: This makes his care conditional on behaviour change, which isn't a decision you can make.

options.text: Leave it, as the final decision is the consultant's.
options.detailed: The consultant decides, but you can still raise a concern about the basis of the decision.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you challenge judgements about a patient's lifestyle while recognising legitimate clinical considerations.
explanation.keyDetails: He smokes. He needs a cardiac procedure. The consultant's comment is about deserving, not clinical benefit.
explanation.reasoning: [A] refocuses on clinical benefit, [B] supports his health, and [D] challenges the judgement. The distractors agree ([C]), undermine the team ([E]), escalate disproportionately ([F]), impose conditions ([G]), or stay silent ([H]).
explanation.competing: [G] might seem helpful for his health, but making treatment conditional isn't your decision.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 2, treating patients fairly, without judgements about lifestyle.
